_note: One shape for every setting an admin changes, on every engine. The founder instructed on 15 September 2026: "All the questions you are asking please factor them as the admin setup on config so that they are dynamic." So an open policy question stops being a question to the founder and becomes a setting: a proposed default, the bounds an admin may set it within, a reason and an audited history for every change, and a screen to change it on. This file holds the shape, the rules every setting obeys and the sentences a change is refused in. Each engine declares its own settings in its own contract, under a settings block in this shape, and never holds another engine's number. packages/engines/src/settings enforces the rules once, for the engine runtime and for the web preview alike, and scripts/check-boundaries.mjs holds every contract to the shape. Nothing here is a real service: a change reaches the engine runtime on loopback, or the tab's memory in the preview, and no phone, desk or patient is told.
why: "All the questions you are asking please factor them as the admin setup on config so that they are dynamic." The shape itself — the types, the rules and the routes — is the Platform Settings lead's proposal under that instruction, and every bound and allowed value in an engine's block says whether somebody decided it.
_sourcesNote: Every contract that holds a settings block, and the engine that owns it. packages/engines/src/settings/blocks.ts imports exactly these, and the build fails on a settings block in a contract this list does not name. An engine adding its first setting adds its contract here.

block.why: What the engine's group is called on the Configuration screen.
One sentence saying what the group decides, in the words somebody in the office would use.
The settings, each in the shape below.

{ version, changelog }: every change to a default in the contract, replayed by the build from nothing, as packages/catalog/gilbert-emergency-terms.json is. A running admin change is not here; it is in the engine's history.

setting.why: Lower case and hyphenated, unique within the engine. It is what a change names and what the history records.
The setting's name on the screen.
The question the setting answers, as a sentence. A number that loses its question quietly becomes the policy.
The engine whose contract holds it. An engine never holds another engine's number.
One of the types below.
What the value is counted in, as the type requires, or null for a type that has none.
{ value } with its provenance: decided (decidedBy, decidedOn, why) or a proposal (decidedBy null, proposedBy, proposedBecause).

The role or the capability in packages/catalog/vetting.json that may change it, or { fromSetting } naming a roleList setting on the same engine. The change route's callers are exactly the roles this resolves to.
What a change reaches, as a sentence. The rule is that a change applies only to what starts after it and never alters something already under way; a setting that does otherwise says so and says why.

{ lowest, highest }, each { value } with its provenance, for a type whose limits are bounds. A moneyCents setting also carries citedFrom, the contract path of the range a document gives, or notCitedBecause.
true or false, for a count or a percentage: whether nought is refused. Minutes and money are always above nought and do not carry it.
For an enum, and optionally a boolean: each value that may be chosen, { value, label } with its provenance.
For text: { value } in characters, with its provenance.
For text: [{ words, why }], sentences no rewording may drop. The way a guardrail on wording is written as a rule rather than trusted.
For a roleList: { roles } from the vetting register, with its provenance.

For a schedule: [{ id, label, role }], the positions a rota is made of, each held by a role on the vetting register. A rota names posts, never people. A post no role on the register holds yet is written { id, label, role: null, roleMissing }, with a sentence saying so: it stays on the rota, no window may name it, and whatever reaches it goes to the next post rather than to a role it was never given.
For a schedule: [{ post, days, from, to, why }], hours that must always have that post on them.
For a list: the type of every item — minutes, count, moneyCents, percentage, enum or text — whose limits the setting carries as it would for one value.
For a list or a roleList: { lowest, highest }, how many items or roles, each with its provenance. A roleList that must always name somebody says so here.
For a record: [{ key, label, type, ... }], a few values that only make sense changed together, each with the limits its type needs.

For a clinical-scope setting: the vetting capability whose holder must confirm a change. Until then the value is in force and shown everywhere it matters as not clinically reviewed; a reviewer confirms through the engine's review route.

{ statement, forbids }: what no value may do, and values that must always be refused. The build runs every forbidden value through the same rules a change goes through and fails if one is accepted, so a guardrail is bounds and type rules rather than trust.

provenance.why: A decided value names who decided it, on what day and why, in the shape packages/catalog/consent.json gives maximumExpiryDecision. A proposal keeps decidedBy: null and says who proposed it and why, so a number cannot become policy by having the question deleted around it. A decided value may keep who proposed it. A clinical-scope default reviewed before it shipped names the reviewer and the day.

types.why: A time a desk waits, an offer lasts or a window stays open. Nought is never a time anybody meant.

How many of something: characters, hours, call-outs. Whether nought is allowed is the setting's, because nought call-outs is a plan with no call-outs and nought characters is a thread nobody can write in.
An amount of money in whole cents. Its bounds come from a range a document gives, cited, where one does.
A whole-number share of a hundred.
On or off. A guardrail on a boolean leaves the forbidden side out of allowed.
One of a few named choices, each with a label and a reason it may be chosen.
Wording patients or nurses read. Never empty, never longer than its maximum, and never without a sentence it must keep.
Roles from packages/catalog/vetting.json, each once. Never a person.
A rota: windows of a post, days and hours. Hours are 00:00 to 24:00 and a window ends after it starts, so a night shift is two windows. Never a named person.
A list of one of minutes, count, moneyCents, percentage, enum or text, each item held to the setting's limits.

A few values that only make sense changed together, like a number of call-outs and the period they are counted over. Changed separately, the first change alone would be in force for a moment it was never meant to be.

rules.statement: Every change says why, and the reason is recorded beside who made it.
A change is made against the settings version the admin was looking at, or not at all.
A value is inside its bounds, one of its allowed values, its allowed roles or posts, and its list length.
A value whose type demands it is above nought, asked before its bounds so that bounds set wrongly cannot let nought through.
A change changes the value in force.
Every role a setting names is a role on the vetting register.
Wording keeps every sentence it must keep.
A rota covers every window it must cover.
The history is added to and never updated or deleted, and what is in force is always the defaults with it replayed in version order.
Something that has started keeps the settings version it started with, and nothing already under way reads a setting again.

read.summary: Read this engine's settings in force, each with its default and provenance, its limits and review state, and every change made to them.

response.why: The version in force. A change is made against it, and whatever starts now keeps it.

Each setting: its key, type, unit, the value in force and the version that set it, its default and provenance, its limits, who may change it, what a change reaches, its guardrail, and its clinical review.

fields.why: The setting's key, which a change names.
Its name on the Configuration screen.
The question it answers, as a sentence.
One of the types above.
What the value is counted in, or null for a type that has none.
The value in force: a number, a switch, a word, a list, a rota or a record, as its type gives.
The settings version that set the value in force, 1 for the contract's default.
The contract's default, of the same kind as the value in force.
Who decided the default, when and why, or who proposed it and why, and who reviewed it where somebody did.
What an admin may set — the bounds, allowed values, roles, posts, items or parts its type carries — with their provenance.
The roles that may change it, resolved from the contract and the settings in force.
What a change reaches, as a sentence.
The sentence no value may break, or null for a setting with none.
The capability whose holder confirms its clinical review, or null for a setting that waits on nobody.
Who confirmed the clinical review of the value in force, or null while it is not clinically reviewed.
The reviewer's reference.
When the review was confirmed through the review route, or null for a default reviewed before it shipped.
The day a default was reviewed before it shipped, or null for a review confirmed through the route.

response.why: Every accepted change, oldest first: which setting, from, to, who, when and why. Nothing in it is edited or removed.

fields.why: The version this change made.
The setting it changed.
The value before, of the kind its type gives.
The value after.
Why, as it was written.
The role of the person who made it.
The reference of the person who made it, from the caller the runtime admitted.
When it was made.

change.summary: Change one setting, with a reason, against the version in force. It applies to what starts after it.

request.why: Chosen by the caller. The same key twice is the same change once, and the history gains one row.
The setting's key, from the settings block of the engine's own contract.
The new value, for a setting in minutes, a count, cents or a percentage.
The new value, for a setting that is on or off.
The new value, for a setting that is one of a few named choices.
The new wording, for a setting patients or nurses read.
The new roles, for a setting that names roles from packages/catalog/vetting.json.
The new rota, for a setting that is windows of a post, days and hours. A post, never a named person.
The new values, for a setting that is a list.
The new values, for a setting whose parts change together.
Why. Asked for by the handler rather than the binder, so that a change without one is refused in its own sentence rather than the general one for a missing field.
The settings version the admin was looking at. A change against an older one is refused.

response.why: When it took effect. Whatever started before it keeps the version it started under.

change.emitsNoneBecause: No engine acts on a settings change. The engine that owns a setting reads the value in force when it starts something, and the event contract refuses an event nobody subscribes to. A change is the row it appends to the engine's own history, which the read route returns.

review.summary: Confirm the clinical review of the value in force for a setting that waits on one.

request.why: Chosen by the caller. The same key twice is the same confirmation once.
The setting's key, from the settings block of the engine's own contract.

The version that set the value being confirmed: 1 for the contract's default, or the version of the change. A reviewer confirms a value they read, never whatever happens to be in force when the request lands.
Why the value is clinically safe. Asked for by the handler, so a confirmation without one is refused in its own sentence.

review.emitsNoneBecause: A confirmation changes no value, so nothing acts differently because of it. It is the row it appends to the engine's own reviews, which the read route returns.

refusals.statement: Only somebody who may change these settings reads them and who changed them.
refusals.why: The history names the people who changed how an engine behaves. It is read by the roles that may change it.

refusals.statement: Only the role a setting names changes it, and the change is recorded against a named person.
refusals.why: A setting decides how the platform treats people. The role or capability the setting names changes it, and a change is recorded against somebody who can be asked about it; everybody else only reads what is in force.

refusals.statement: There is no setting by that name.
refusals.why: An unknown setting is refused rather than stored, or the history fills with changes nothing reads.

refusals.statement: A change to a setting says why, or it is not made.
refusals.why: The history is read after something has gone wrong. A change with no reason is a number somebody moved.

refusals.statement: These settings changed after you opened them. Read what is in force now and decide against that.
refusals.why: Two admins changing one setting from screens opened at the same time would each overwrite a decision they never saw.

refusals.statement: That is not the kind of value this setting holds.
refusals.why: A word where a number belongs, or a list where one choice belongs, is a guess at what the admin meant, and a setting is never set by a guess.

refusals.statement: This setting is never nought or less, whatever its range says.
refusals.why: A wait of nothing, an offer that lapses as it is made and a fee of nothing are never what anybody meant. The range is a proposal and could be set wrongly; this refusal does not depend on it.

refusals.statement: Every role a setting names is a role on the vetting register.
refusals.why: A role the register does not hold is a gate nobody can be vetted through, which looks like a shortage rather than a mistake.

refusals.statement: That wording is longer than this setting allows.
refusals.why: The maximum is the space the words are read in. Wording that does not fit is cut off where somebody reads it.

refusals.statement: That wording drops a sentence this setting must always keep.
refusals.why: Some wording carries a promise that protects somebody. It may be reworded around that sentence and never without it.

refusals.statement: That rota leaves hours uncovered that must always have somebody on them.
refusals.why: A rota with a gap is an alert with nobody to go to, and nobody finds out until one arrives.

refusals.statement: That is outside what an admin may set for this setting.
refusals.why: The bounds, the allowed values and the allowed roles sit beside the default in the engine's contract. Moving a setting past them is a change to that contract, not a setting.

refusals.statement: That is already the value in force, so there is nothing to change.
refusals.why: A change that changes nothing is a row in the history saying something happened when nothing did.

refusals.statement: Only somebody holding the capability this setting names confirms its clinical review, and the confirmation is recorded against a named person.
refusals.why: A clinical-scope setting decides who may do what to a patient. Confirming it is a clinician's act, attributed like a signed review.

refusals.statement: There is no setting by that name.
refusals.why: An unknown setting is refused rather than stored, or the reviews fill with confirmations of nothing.

refusals.statement: This setting does not wait on a clinical review.
refusals.why: A confirmation of a setting nobody asked a clinician about reads, later, as if one had been needed.

refusals.statement: A clinical review says why the value is safe, or it is not recorded.
refusals.why: A confirmation with no reason is a signature under nothing.

refusals.statement: That is not the value in force for this setting. Review what is in force now.
refusals.why: A reviewer confirms the value they read. A value replaced since is not the one patients are being treated under.

refusals.statement: That value has already been clinically reviewed.
refusals.why: Two confirmations of one value are one review recorded twice.

refusals.statement: Nobody confirms the clinical review of a change they made themselves.
refusals.why: packages/catalog/vetting.json's selfActionRefusals, applied to settings: a review by the person who made the change is no review.

screen.blurb: Every setting the engines work to: what is in force, who decided it, what an admin may set, and every change with its reason.
screen.intro: Each setting says what is in force, its default and who decided it, what an admin may set, what a change reaches and what no value may do. A change is reviewed before it is confirmed, and every change is kept with who made it and why.
screen.preview: This preview keeps changes in this tab's memory and nowhere else. No phone, desk or patient is told, and a reload puts the defaults back.
screen.searchHelp: By its name, what it decides or the engine that owns it.
screen.roles: Only these roles may be named: {roles}
screen.postWithoutRole: {post}, which no role on the vetting register holds yet
screen.limitsAreProposals: What an admin may set is a proposal nobody has decided.
screen.limitsDecided: What an admin may set was decided.
screen.limitsPartlyDecided: Some of what an admin may set was decided; the rest is a proposal nobody has decided.
screen.reviewWaitsOn: Waits on somebody who may {capability} to confirm it, from the engine's review route.
screen.reasonHelp: Written into the history beside your name. It is read when somebody asks why the platform behaved as it did.
screen.historyEmpty: Nothing has been changed from the default yet.
screen.historyNeverEdited: Every change is added here with who made it, when and why. Nothing here is edited or removed.
screen.operationsNote: How long the safety desk waits, and what an admin may set it to, is on the Configuration tab with every other setting.

editors.list: New values in {unit}, smallest first, separated by commas

howToChange: An engine's settings live in its own contract, under settings, in this shape. Add the contract to sources here the first time it has one.

Change a default in the setting's own default block, never in code, and add a changelog entry to that contract's settings.defaults: the next version, the day, who by role, every setting changed as { setting, from, to }, and why. npm run check replays the changelog from nothing and fails if it does not arrive at the defaults.

A decided default names who decided it, on what day and why. A default nobody decided keeps decidedBy: null and says who proposed it and why. So does every bound, allowed value, maximum length, allowed role list and list length.
Every default sits inside its own limits, and every value a guardrail forbids is refused by the same rules a change goes through.

Declare the engine's read and change routes in packages/catalog/apis/<engine>.json to the shapes in routes above, word for word, with every refusal above for that route, and append them to apis.lock. A setting with reviewRequired needs the review route too. Mark a route built only when the engine binds it through packages/engines/src/settings.

Whatever an engine starts with a setting keeps the settings version it started with. Read the value in force when something starts, keep it on the thing started, and never read it again for that thing.
